passages.happening:
Jacob reaches “the land of the people of the east” (verse 1). He sees a well in a field, with three flocks of sheep lying near it. A large stone covers its mouth (verse 2). The shepherds wait until all the flocks are gathered, then roll the stone away together (verse 3).

The shepherds say they are from Haran, and they know Laban (verses 4-5). “Here comes his daughter Rachel with his sheep” (verse 6).

Jacob tells them to water the sheep now. They answer that they cannot until all the flocks are there (verses 7-8). Then Rachel arrives, “for she was a shepherdess” (verse 9). Jacob goes up, rolls the stone away by himself, and waters his uncle's sheep (verse 10).

“Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud” (verse 11). He tells her who he is, and she runs to tell her father (verse 12). Laban runs out, embraces him, kisses him and brings him home (verse 13). “You are indeed my own flesh and blood,” Laban says (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This is the Bethel promise at work. God said, ‘I will watch over you wherever you go’ (28:15). Jacob walks hundreds of miles and arrives at the one well where his cousin is coming with her flock. God is not named, but the reader sees his hand.

A meeting at a well is a scene the first hearers knew. Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well (chapter 24), and Moses will meet his wife at one (Exodus 2). The reader expects a wedding.

Wells in that land were shared and guarded. The heavy stone kept the water clean and stopped any one shepherd from taking more than his share. So the custom was to wait and move it together. Jacob, seeing Rachel, rolls it off alone. It is a show of strength, and of feeling.

Then he weeps. He has been alone since he left home. Now he has found family. A kiss of greeting between relatives was normal in that world. The tears are his own.

Laban ‘ran’ to meet him. Years before, Laban rushed out to meet Abraham's servant once he had seen the gold (24:29-30). This time Jacob has no camels and no gold. Laban's welcome is warm. What he does next will show his heart.
passages.later:
Moses' meeting at a well follows the same pattern: he helps a woman water her father's flock, and marries into the family (Exodus 2:16-21).

Jesus meets a woman at Jacob's well in Samaria and offers her living water (John 4:5-14). John notes that the well was ‘Jacob's well’ (John 4:6).
passages.asks: God led Jacob to the right well before Jacob even knew to look for it. Ask where you can see, looking back, that you were guided before you knew it. Then ask whether you trust that same care for the road ahead.

passages.happening:
After a month, Laban says, “Just because you are my relative, should you work for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be” (verse 15).

“Now Laban had two daughters; the older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel” (verse 16). “Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful” (verse 17).

Jacob loves Rachel. “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel,” he says (verse 18). Laban answers, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me” (verse 19).

“So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
In that world a groom's family normally gave a gift or payment to the bride's family. Abraham's servant brought gold, silver and clothing for Rebekah (24:53). Jacob arrived with nothing. So he offers the one thing he has: his work. Seven years is a very high price, and verse 20 says why.

The text calls the sisters ‘the older’ and ‘the younger’. In Hebrew these are the same words used of Esau and Jacob in chapter 27. The reader should notice. The older and the younger are about to be switched again.

Leah's eyes are called ‘weak’. The Hebrew word can also mean ‘tender’ or ‘soft’. Readers are not sure whether it means a flaw or something gentle about her. Either way, Rachel is the one Jacob sees.

Notice Laban's answer. He never actually says yes. ‘Better that I give her to you than to another’ sounds like agreement. It is not quite a promise.

Seven years ‘seemed but a few days because of his love for her’. This is one of the tenderest lines in Genesis. Rebekah told Jacob to stay with Laban ‘for a while’, literally ‘a few days’ (27:44). The same words return here, and the few days have become seven years.
passages.later:
The Song of Songs speaks of love that cannot be bought: “If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned” (Song of Songs 8:7). Jacob does not buy Rachel. He gives seven years because he loves her.

Paul writes that love “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).
passages.asks: Jacob's seven years felt like a few days because he loved Rachel. Ask what you would wait for, and work for, because you love it. Then ask what your waiting shows about what you love most.

passages.happening:
The seven years end. “Grant me my wife,” Jacob says (verse 21). Laban gathers the men of the place and makes a feast (verse 22).

“But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her” (verse 23). Laban gives his servant girl Zilpah to Leah as her maidservant (verse 24).

“When morning came, there was Leah! ‘What have you done to me?’ Jacob said to Laban. ‘Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?’” (verse 25).

Laban replies, “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older” (verse 26). He tells Jacob to finish the week's celebration, and then Rachel will be his too, “in return for another seven years of work” (verse 27).

Jacob agrees. After the week, Laban gives him Rachel, and gives his servant girl Bilhah to Rachel as her maidservant (verses 28-29). Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The man who deceived his blind father in the dark of old age is now deceived in the dark of his wedding night. He who put on his brother's clothes is given a bride he cannot see. The text makes no comment. The echoes say enough.

‘Why have you deceived me?’ uses the same Hebrew word Isaac used of Jacob: ‘Your brother came deceitfully’ (27:35). And Laban's answer stings. ‘Here we do not give the younger before the older.’ The word for the older daughter means ‘the firstborn’, the very right Jacob took from Esau.

How could this happen? A wedding feast lasted a week, as Samson's did (Judges 14:12). The Hebrew word for ‘feast’ comes from the verb ‘to drink’. The bride was brought to the groom after dark, and was probably veiled, as Rebekah veiled herself before Isaac (24:65). Laban's custom about older daughters may have been real. But he had seven years to mention it.

Two women are handed over in this passage who are not asked anything. Zilpah and Bilhah are enslaved women. Laban gives them away as wedding gifts, as part of what went with each daughter into her marriage. They have no say. In the next chapter they will be given to Jacob to bear children, and the text will show what that cost them.

And there is Leah. She was put in her sister's place by her father, in the dark, and woke up married to a man who wanted someone else. Whatever she knew or agreed to, the text does not say. It says only what Jacob felt in the morning. The rest of the chapter turns to what Leah felt.
passages.later:
Israel's law later forbade this marriage: “You must not take your wife’s sister as a rival wife and have sexual relations with her while your wife is still alive” (Leviticus 18:18). It also ruled for the son of an unloved wife: “If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other unloved” (Deuteronomy 21:15), he must still give the firstborn's rights to the true firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:16-17).

When Jesus was asked about marriage, he went back to Genesis 2: “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female’” (Matthew 19:4), and “the two will become one flesh” (Matthew 19:5).

Paul writes, “Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return” (Galatians 6:7).
passages.hard:
Does the Bible approve of a man marrying two sisters, or having more than one wife?

Genesis describes Jacob's marriages. It never commends them. Genesis sets out one man and one woman at creation (2:24). Every household in Genesis with more than one wife, from Lamech (4:19-24) to Abraham with Sarah and Hagar to Jacob, is marked by rivalry and grief. This chapter's sympathy is with Leah, the wife pushed aside, and the next chapter shows the sisters turning childbirth into a contest. Israel's law later forbade taking a wife's sister as a rival wife (Leviticus 18:18). Jesus, asked about marriage, went back to Genesis 2.

Some readers have taken God's blessing on this family as approval of how it was formed. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, answer that God works through this family because he promised to, not because its arrangements are a model. Already in the Middle Ages the Jewish teacher Nachmanides asked how Jacob could marry two sisters when the law forbids it, and gave his own answer. The question is old.

The narrator's silence is not praise. The story itself shows the misery: a husband who loves one wife and not the other, sisters set against each other, children named for their mother's pain.
passages.asks: Jacob tasted his own medicine on his wedding night. Ask whether you have ever been hurt by the very thing you once did to someone else. Then ask what that might teach you, not about getting even, but about what you did.

passages.happening:
“When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren” (verse 31).

Leah has a son and names him Reuben, “for she said, ‘The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now’” (verse 32).

She has a second son: “Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well.” She names him Simeon (verse 33).

She has a third: “Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” He is named Levi (verse 34).

And a fourth: “This time I will praise the LORD.” She names him Judah. Then she stops having children for a time (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
‘Unloved’ is literally ‘hated’. In Hebrew, love and hate side by side often mean choosing one over the other, as the note on Genesis 25:19-26 explains. Verse 30 has just said Jacob loved Rachel ‘more than Leah’. But Leah does not hear a comparison. She hears that she is not loved. And the LORD sees it.

This is the first time God is named in the chapter. He is named because of Leah.

Each son's name is a sound-play on what Leah felt, a small prayer in a name.

Reuben sounds like ‘See, a son’. Leah says, ‘The LORD has seen my affliction.’ Affliction is the word used when God heard Hagar (16:11) and when he saw Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:7). Then her hope: ‘Surely my husband will love me now.’ He does not.

Simeon sounds like ‘he has heard’. ‘The LORD has heard that I am unloved.’ She says the word about herself now.

Levi sounds like ‘attached’ or ‘joined’. ‘Now at last my husband will become attached to me.’ Still hoping.

Judah sounds like ‘praise’. ‘This time I will praise the LORD.’ For the first time, Leah's son's name says nothing about her husband. Her hope has turned from Jacob to God.

The unloved wife becomes the mother of Levi, from whom Israel's priests come, and of Judah, from whom King David comes. Genesis does not say so yet. But the first hearers knew.
passages.later:
Matthew's family line of Jesus runs through Leah's son: “Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers” (Matthew 1:2). Revelation calls the risen Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

God sees the overlooked, as he saw Hagar: “You are the God who sees me” (Genesis 16:13). Paul writes, “God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). And a psalm says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18).

Leah is buried in the family grave at Machpelah. Jacob asks to be buried there too, saying, “there I buried Leah” (Genesis 49:31). Rachel, the loved wife, is buried by the road to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19).
passages.hard: A word for anyone who has felt like Leah: unloved in a marriage, or second in a home, or chosen by no one. God saw Leah when her husband did not. Your sorrow is seen too, and it is not the measure of your worth. If you are carrying this, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are not safe at home, the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Leah named three sons for her hope that her husband would love her, and the fourth for praise to God. Ask whose love you are waiting on to feel that you are worth something. Then ask what it would mean to say, with Leah, ‘This time I will praise the LORD.’
